overview: This atlas label groups several societies in what is now Peru between 1279 and 1492. It names neither one people nor one empire. Its repeated outline includes Chincha, Túcume and Kuélap but cannot show their changing frontiers or the Inca expansion. Regional communities flourished after Wari and before Inca rule; each had its own institutions and material traditions. Wari, Tiwanaku, Chimú and Inca history belong to distinct accounts.

periods.title: Regional powers within an atlas outline
periods.summary: The map begins during a much longer era of regional communities. Its 1279 boundary is an imported snapshot, not a common foundation date for the societies discussed here.

periods.title: Changing rulers on the northern coast
periods.summary: At Túcume, archaeological remodeling accompanies the period conventionally associated with Chimú conquest around 1375. This local sequence cannot be applied as a single political history to every part of the polygon.

periods.title: Inca expansion and an unfinished story
periods.summary: Túcume came under Inca power around 1470. The atlas continues to repeat its umbrella outline until 1492, obscuring these changing political relationships rather than documenting a surviving independent federation.

items.text: Chincha linked the coast and highlands through trade. Later colonial accounts describe specialized merchants traveling by coastal raft and llama caravan, alongside farming and fishing communities. In the fifteenth century, Inca rulers incorporated Chincha while allowing its leaders considerable status. Commercial influence could survive a change of overlord.

At Monte Sierpe in the Pisco Valley, researchers mapped roughly 5,200 pits. One charcoal sample dates between 1320 and 1405. A group arranged as six rows of seven plus eight more pits totals fifty: ancient organization that still invites a little arithmetic. Researchers propose that this place helped organize storage and exchange.

Tiny plant traces bring food and packaging into the story. Monte Sierpe sediments contained maize evidence and bulrush pollen. Researchers suggest goods may have arrived in plant-fiber bundles, mats or baskets. The pits reveal possible handling and storage practices, although plant traces alone cannot reconstruct a complete market day.

Túcume was a center of Lambayeque power that later served Chimú and Inca rulers. Its twenty-six adobe pyramids formed an extensive built landscape. Excavators identified successive rebuilding and recovered painted walls and sculpted marine designs. These changes allow archaeologists to study conquest alongside local artistic continuity.

sections.title: Homes, water and care in particular communities

items.text: A Túcume pyramid was more than a solid mound. The municipality describes elite residential buildings with storerooms, patios, decorated rooms, ramps and kitchens. People moved between work, ceremony and rest inside these complexes. These are features of the long-lived site; individual rooms need excavation dates before we can assign them to one ruler.

Kuélap, high above the Utcubamba Valley, centered on a settlement atop a massive stone-walled platform. The name Chachapoya groups communities described by later Inca and Spanish outsiders. Researchers still debate Kuélap’s political and religious role. Its imposing walls do not establish that every building was military or that the whole region obeyed one king.

Kuélap contained hundreds of residential structures and agricultural land. It was a place where people lived, not simply a monument visited for ceremonies. Archaeological research places its occupation across the centuries before Inca rule and into the Inca period. The surviving buildings let us ask how everyday work fitted around immense communal construction.

Some people at Kuélap were buried beneath house floors; others lay in wall spaces or collective tombs. The living and the dead could therefore share the same built environment. These varied arrangements help researchers investigate social belonging and status, but a shared burial location does not by itself prove that everyone was a biological relative.

Keeping water moving mattered in this forested mountain setting. A 2019 aerial laser survey revealed subtle features in Kuélap’s Imperio sector that researchers identify as parts of planned drainage. The survey helps conservation teams see structures hidden by vegetation. These are drainage observations, not evidence for a town-wide toilet or sewer system.

Skulls from Kuélap’s Revash collection, assigned to roughly 1350 to 1470, preserve openings made by trepanation, a form of skull surgery. Some show bone healing, meaning people survived after the operation. The study could link only one case clearly to a traumatic injury; the reasons for most procedures remain uncertain. Individual excavation contexts in this old collection are incomplete.

sections.title: A surviving record, and the knowledge to read it

items.text: A genuine record-keeping example is the cotton-cord khipu from Chulpaca in Ica, now Smithsonian catalog 14/3866. The museum attributes it to probable Inca use and places it broadly between 1450 and 1532, partly beyond this map’s endpoint. Knots and dyed cords carried information. Its catalog supplies no decoded message, so an invented sentence would misrepresent this object.

Inca cord keepers used numerical knowledge that scholars can partly recover. Manuel Medrano illustrates 2,035 with two knots in the thousands position, none in the hundreds, three in the tens, and a five-turn long knot for the units. This is a modern teaching example of the convention, not a reading of the Chulpaca object. Many meanings beyond numbers remain unresolved.

ending.text: There was no single fall of all these societies in 1492. Túcume’s succession of Lambayeque, Chimú and Inca authority illustrates one local transformation. Communities and knowledge continued under changed institutions; khipu use, for example, persisted after the Spanish conquest. The atlas cutoff closes a map category, not the lives of its peoples.
